source2: M. Sinclair F. Hood, Aegean civilization: Period of the Early Palaces in Crete, Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Aegean-civilization/Period-of-the-Early-Palaces-in-Crete-c-2000-1700
notes: End of MM II: an earthquake leveled Knossos c. 1720 BCE; palaces were rebuilt on a grander scale and palatial society continued into the Neopalatial period. Both sources are Britannica (not independent); violent destruction is a minority alternative.

source1: Colette Hemingway and Sean Hemingway, Minoan Crete, Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art - https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/minoan-crete
notes: Widespread LM IB destructions c. 1450 BCE; Mycenaean Greeks then controlled Knossos, Linear B replacing Linear A (foreign elite as rulers). Whether Mycenaeans caused the destructions or exploited internal upheaval is debated. High chronology puts them c. 1470.

source1: Akinori Uesugi, An Overview on the Iron Age in South Asia, in A. Uesugi (ed.), Iron Age in South Asia, Kansai University, 2018 - https://www.academia.edu/37419677/An_Overview_on_the_Iron_Age_in_South_Asia
notes: Southern Neolithic gave way gradually: black-and-red ware at Sanganakallu c. 1400 BCE, iron at Hallur c. 1200 BCE; transition called complex and possibly gradual, with a hiatus at some sites (Ramapuram). Single source, low confidence.

source1: Akinori Uesugi, An Overview on the Iron Age in South Asia, in A. Uesugi (ed.), Iron Age in South Asia, Kansai University, 2018 - https://www.academia.edu/37419677/An_Overview_on_the_Iron_Age_in_South_Asia
notes: No recorded central authority. Megalithic tradition continued to about the start of the Common Era while Bindusara extended Mauryan rule into the Deccan (to Karnataka); Asokan edict at Brahmagiri. Political incorporation without material or population break.
